meta.location: The court of king Noah, in the land of Lehi-Nephi
meta.date: ~148 BC (Decalogue quoted at v. 12–24, given ~1300 BC)

world_behind.title: The face that shone
world_behind.text: Verse 5 draws the comparison itself: Abinadi's face shone as Moses' did in the mount. Exodus reports the same phenomenon three times and has Moses veil himself afterward. The record does not leave the reader to notice the parallel; it names Moses in the verse.

world_behind.title: Recited from memory
world_behind.text: Abinadi is a prisoner in a council chamber, and the record does not say that anyone handed him a book. What verses 12 through 24 preserve is likely a man reciting Exodus 20 from memory, in a colony whose copy of the law was engraved on brass and kept by the priests he is addressing.

world_behind.title: The versification differs
world_behind.text: Verse 22 carries two commandments that Exodus separates into two verses. The versification here appears to follow the block as Abinadi delivered it rather than the chapter-and-verse arrangement of a Bible.

world_behind.title: The standard charge against a prophet
world_behind.text: "Away with this fellow" and "he is mad." A crowd said the first of Jesus (Luke 23:18) and a Roman governor said the second of Paul (Acts 26:24). Noah reaches for both in a single line before any argument has been offered.

world_behind.title: A law explained as a concession
world_behind.text: Abinadi says the law was given because Israel was stiffnecked, quick to iniquity, and slow to remember. The strictness answered that condition. Deuteronomy makes a similar move about divorce, and Paul about the law as a schoolmaster. The reasoning is old and the record states it plainly.

world_behind.title: Jeremiah, inverted
world_behind.text: Verse 11 says the commandments are not written in the priests' hearts (Jer. 31:33). Jeremiah's new covenant is a law written in the heart. Abinadi reads from stone precisely because the writing did not take.

world_behind.title: The law given an expiry
world_behind.text: Verse 27 says the time will come when it is no longer expedient to keep the law of Moses. That is said to men who claim to teach it, by a man who has just recited it in full, and it is the sharpest statement on the subject in this record.

words.text: Astonishment, without the modern sense of curiosity. Abinadi says his words fill them with wonder, amazement, and anger: three reactions in ascending order, and the first two are involuntary. The court is described as impressed against its will.

Carved, and the same verb this record uses of engraving on plates. Treated at 1 Nephi 20:5. The commandment forbids a carved likeness, and the man reciting it is part of a people whose scripture exists only because someone carved it. The record never remarks on the overlap.

A legal word: not merely innocent in feeling but not held liable. Treated at Mosiah 4:25. The commandment Abinadi recites says the Lord will not hold guiltless the man who takes his name in vain. The court had used that word of itself in the previous chapter, assuring Noah that they were guiltless and that he had not sinned. Abinadi is reading a list these men claim to teach, and this line of it names who decides the question and on what ground.

Not an unfamiliar person. Treated at Mosiah 5:13. In the law a stranger is a foreigner living among you, and the phrase "thy stranger that is within thy gates" (v. 18) assumes he is a fixture of the household's world. The sabbath commandment keeps widening its list until it has covered the son, the daughter, both servants, the cattle, and him. Abinadi recites it to a court supported by a fifth part of everything their people owned. The commandment gives a day off to a man's ox.

cites.quote: thy stranger that is within thy gates

spans.text: thy stranger that is within thy gates

words.text: To desire what belongs to another. It is the only commandment in the list that governs an interior state rather than an act, and it comes last, after a catalogue of the neighbor's property. Nothing in the verse requires the coveting to produce anything.

Tightly drawn, allowing no slack. Abinadi calls the law given to Israel "a very strict law" and says the strictness was a response to the people, who were stiffnecked, quick to do iniquity, slow to remember. The severity is explained by their condition.

phrases.term: Away with this fellow, and slay him; for... he is mad
phrases.text: Two dismissals in one breath, and neither engages the message. A crowd used the first of Jesus before Pilate (Luke 23:18); a governor used the second of Paul mid-defense (Acts 26:24). Noah does not argue that Abinadi is wrong, only that he is contemptible and unwell.

phrases.term: Touch me not, for God shall smite you if ye lay your hands upon me
phrases.text: A prohibition with a reason and a limit. The reason is that the message is unfinished; the limit is "at this time." What Abinadi claims is a delay, and the chapter's last chapters make that limit matter.

phrases.term: His face shone with exceeding luster, even as Moses' did while in the mount of Sinai
phrases.text: The record supplying its own cross-reference. The people durst not touch him, and the reason given is the Spirit upon him and the light on his face. It is the only physical protection anyone in this record receives, and the record describes it in a lone clause.

phrases.term: Then it matters not whither I go, if it so be that I am saved
phrases.text: The whole of Abinadi's position on his own survival. He has just been told he cannot be killed yet; his response is that the timing is not his concern. The sentence is spoken by a man who will be burned four chapters later and it does not change.

phrases.term: What you do with me, after this, shall be as a type and a shadow of things which are to come
phrases.text: A prophet identifying his own death as a figure before it happens. The phrase occurs once in scripture. Abinadi is not predicting the manner of his death; he is telling his killers that whatever they choose will signify something, which puts the meaning outside their control.

phrases.term: I perceive that they are not written in your hearts
phrases.text: The reason given for reading the commandments aloud. Jeremiah's promise (Jer. 31:33) was a law written in the heart instead of on stone; Abinadi reads from stone because the interior version is missing. The next clause is harder. They have studied and taught iniquity most of their lives.

phrases.term: Wherefore the Lord blessed the sabbath day, and hallowed it
phrases.text: The sabbath rationale, and something is missing from it. Exodus gives six days of making and then rest on the seventh (Ex. 20:11), and grounds the blessing in the rest. This recitation keeps the making and the blessing and drops the resting, the one substantive variant in the whole block.

phrases.term: The time shall come when it shall no more be expedient to keep the law of Moses
phrases.text: Said to men who teach that law, immediately after reciting it in full. Abinadi grants that keeping it is expedient "as yet" and then puts a term on it. The phrase appears once in scripture and it is the hinge between this chapter and the next.

phrases.term: Salvation doth not come by the law alone
phrases.text: The word doing the work is "alone." Abinadi does not deny the law's role; he denies its sufficiency. The same sentence supplies what is missing: the atonement God himself shall make. Without it, the verse says, they must unavoidably perish notwithstanding the law.

phrases.term: A law of performances and of ordinances
phrases.text: The record's definition of what was given, and it is functional. Things performed and things prescribed, observed strictly, day by day, with a stated purpose: to keep them in remembrance of God and their duty. The law is described as a memory device.

phrases.term: They understood not that there could not any man be saved except it were through the redemption of God
phrases.text: The failure located precisely. They misread what the law was for. Abinadi has just accused the priests of the same thing, so verse 32 is a historical charge and a present one at once.

phrases.term: He, himself, should be oppressed and afflicted
phrases.text: Isaiah's words about the suffering servant (Isa. 53:7), arriving as the last clause of the chapter. Abinadi has moved from the law to the prophets to a person, and the chapter breaks off mid-argument. The sentence continues into Mosiah 14, which is Isaiah 53 entire.

verses.label: v. 1–4
verses.title: The order, and the refusal
verses.text: Away with this fellow, slay him, he is mad. They move to seize him and cannot. His answer is that the message is unfinished, that God will not permit his destruction at this time, and that their anger is at the truth rather than at him.

verses.label: v. 5–9
verses.title: Protected, and finishing
verses.text: The Spirit upon him, his face shining as Moses' did, power and authority in his speech. He tells them they have no power to slay him and therefore he will finish; that his words cut them; that they are filled with wonder, amazement, and anger; and that where he goes afterward does not matter.

verses.label: v. 10–11
verses.title: A figure, and a reason to read
verses.text: What they do with him will be a type and a shadow. And the commandments are not written in their hearts, which is why he will now read them aloud to the men whose profession was teaching them.

verses.label: v. 12–19
verses.title: The law, first table
verses.text: The record reproduces Exodus 20:4–11 with the differences confined to single words. Exodus 20:4 has "any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above"; verse 12 has "any likeness of things which are in heaven above." The rest, including the full household list of Exodus 20:10, "thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy man-servant, nor thy maid-servant, nor thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates," stands word for word. What is missing is the opening of the passage: verse 11 says "I read unto you the remainder of the commandments," so the record reports the first commandment being given without setting it down.

verses.label: v. 20–24
verses.title: The law, second table
verses.text: The record matches Exodus 20:12–17 down to the itemized coveting list, "thy neighbor's house... his man-servant, nor his maid-servant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor anything that is thy neighbor's." The verse divisions differ. Exodus gives adultery and stealing separate verses; verse 22 here puts both in one. Verse 20 also keeps the promise attached to honoring parents, "that thy days may be long upon the land," which is the clause quoted back at 1 Nephi 17:55 by a man refusing worship. A recitation delivered from custody reproduces its source closely enough that its departures can be counted.

verses.label: v. 31–35
verses.title: What it pointed at
verses.text: All these things were types. They did not understand, because of hard hearts, that no one is saved except through the redemption of God. Did Moses not prophesy of the Messiah? Have not all the prophets since the world began? Have they not said God himself would come down, take the form of man, raise the dead, and be oppressed and afflicted?

chapter.title: A prophet is protected precisely long enough
chapter.text: He cannot be touched because the message is unfinished, and he says so. The protection is explicitly temporary and he does not pretend otherwise: "it matters not whither I go." Four chapters later the protection ends on schedule.

chapter.title: The record names its own Moses parallel
chapter.text: Rather than letting the reader notice that a shining face echoes Sinai, verse 5 says Moses out loud. That is unusual for this record, which normally lets its allusions sit unmarked, and it happens at the moment Abinadi begins reciting the law Moses received.

chapter.title: The law is recited to the men paid to teach it
chapter.text: They claimed in the previous chapter to teach the law of Moses (Mosiah 12:28); Abinadi's answer is to read it to them. Thirteen verses of quotation function as a cross-examination exhibit, and the question after it is whether they have taught it.

chapter.title: The one substantive variant is about rest
chapter.text: Everything else in the quoted block is spelling or pronouns. Exodus grounds the sabbath blessing in God having rested; this recitation keeps the six days of making and the blessing and omits the rest. The record does not comment, and neither should a reader who has not weighed how small a change it is.

chapter.title: The law is defined by purpose
chapter.text: Performances, ordinances, strictness, daily observance. The reason given is memory. Once that is established, verse 31 can say the whole thing was types, and verse 32 can say the failure was misunderstanding.

chapter.title: The charge is misreading, in two directions
chapter.text: Ancient Israel did not understand what the law was for; Noah's priests teach it without keeping it. Abinadi indicts a nation's history and a court's practice with the same sentence, and neither is accused of ignorance of the text.

chapter.title: The chapter ends mid-sentence
chapter.text: Verse 35 introduces a servant oppressed and afflicted and stops. What follows in Mosiah 14 is Isaiah 53 entire, so the chapter break falls inside Abinadi's argument.

applications.title: Finish the message
applications.text: Abinadi's whole claim on his own safety was that he had not finished. Identify something true you have started saying and stopped saying, and decide whether the stopping was fear or wisdom.

applications.title: Read it to them
applications.text: When someone claims a standard they are not keeping, the most useful thing may be to state the standard plainly rather than to argue about their conduct.

applications.title: Ask what a practice is for
applications.text: The law is defined here as a memory device with daily observances. Take one religious habit you keep and articulate what it is designed to keep you remembering.

applications.title: Check for "alone"
applications.text: Abinadi did not deny the law; he denied it was sufficient by itself. Where have you taken something good and quietly made it the whole of what you rely on?

applications.title: Notice involuntary wonder
applications.text: The court was filled with wonder and amazement before it got to anger. When something true lands on you and the first response is discomfort, note what came before the discomfort.

applications.title: Let the meaning be outside your control
applications.text: Abinadi told his killers that whatever they chose would signify something. In a situation you cannot control, the choice available is what it will mean.

questions.text: When have I called someone mad rather than answering what they said?
Could I say "it matters not whither I go" about something I am actually afraid of?
Which commandments do I know by heart and have not written on it?
What am I keeping that was meant to be temporary, and what is it pointing at?
Do the things I do strictly still keep me in remembrance, or have they become the whole point?
What have I obeyed for years without understanding what it was for?
